verdicts.evidence: routes.ts:52-61 reads `const result = await insertMessage(...)` … `if (result.outcome === "created") broadcaster.publishMessageCreated(result.message);` … `return c.json(...)`. The insert is awaited on an autocommit connection, so the documented requirement — the row is committed before anyone hears about it — holds; only the two source lines are in the other order. The proposed swap changes nothing observable, because @hono/node-server writes the response only after the handler's promise resolves. Measured both orderings on a real server: `today` (publish, then return c.json) and `proposed` (build the response, publish, return it) each published the frame BEFORE the client's POST resolved in 20/20 runs, median gap 0.21 ms vs 0.17 ms — noise. The consequence the candidate names is the documented design, not a defect: PRD §Real-time delivery says "broadcast to the room (sender included; the client de-duplicates by id)", chat-store.ts:132 `addMessage` returns early when `held.some((kept) => kept.id === message.id)`, and room-chat.tsx:18 `untilTheServerHasIt` drops the optimistic copy the moment the store holds that id. The throwing-publish half has no code behind it: `Broadcaster` (broadcaster.ts:9-10) returns `void`, the only implementation is the in-process hub, whose publish path is `JSON.stringify(frame)` on a Zod-parsed Message plus `ws` `socket.send`, and `ws` throws from send only at readyState CONNECTING (node_modules/ws/lib/websocket.js:400) while the hub only ever receives sockets from the `connection` event (index.ts:26 `sockets.on("connection", (socket) => hub.accept(socket))`), where they are OPEN. LISTEN/NOTIFY and Redis are "documented, not built" (architecture.md §5).
verdicts.fix: None. Nothing in the handler can make the HTTP response reach the wire before the broadcast; only deferring the publish past the response flush would, and that is machinery the PRD does not ask for. If the wording bothers anyone, the doc sentence in architecture.md §5 is the thing to soften ("insert, commit, then announce"), not the code.
verdicts.note: The two statements are in the order the finding says, but the order is unobservable — the response is written after the handler returns either way — and the sender receiving its own echo first is exactly what `addMessage` and `untilTheServerHasIt` are written for.
verdicts.originalIssue: Write routes broadcast before they respond (insert then publish then c.json), while CLAUDE.md and architecture.md section 5 fix the order as insert, respond, then broadcast; rooms/routes.ts:30 has the same inversion.

verdicts.evidence: The query counts are right — I instrumented `Queryable.query`: GET with a cursor issues 3 statements (`SELECT 1 FROM rooms WHERE id = $1`, `SELECT … FROM messages WHERE id = $1 AND room_id = $2`, then the paged read whose `seq > (SELECT seq FROM messages WHERE id = $2 AND room_id = $1)` repeats the lookup), GET without one issues 2. The budget claim is what fails. At the PRD's assumed monthly volume loaded into a single room (50,000 messages, PGlite): backfill p95 1.18-1.75 ms and cold newest page p95 14.3-16.3 ms against NFR-1's 50 ms; `roomExists` measured alone is p95 0.095 ms in-process and 0.227 ms warm, i.e. ~6% of a backfill request and 0.2% of the budget. The "reconnect storm" is not a storm: 50 concurrent backfills of that room finished in 53.1 ms wall clock, ~1 ms each. The cost that actually dominates the read is parsing and serialising the 200-row page, which the suggested fix does not touch. The fix as written also regresses a documented contract: architecture.md §4 says "An unknown room is 404; a cursor this room never held is 400 invalid_cursor", and today an unknown room asked with a valid cursor answers `404 room_not_found` (measured). Dropping `roomExists` on the cursor path turns that into `400 invalid_cursor`, and no test would catch it — routes.test.ts:172 uses `after=latest`, which the query schema rejects with 400 invalid_request before the handler runs.
verdicts.fix: None. Caveat for the record: PGlite runs in-process, so a real Postgres adds a TCP round trip per statement; even at a pessimistic 1 ms per round trip the three-query backfill is ~3 ms against a 50 ms budget, a 15x margin.
verdicts.note: The redundancy is real and the arithmetic is right, but it costs 0.1 ms against a 50 ms budget, and the fix as proposed would answer an unknown room with 400 invalid_cursor instead of the documented 404.

verdicts.evidence: The two round trips are real — instrumenting `query` shows `SELECT 1 FROM rooms WHERE id = $1` then the INSERT — but the guard is not redundant with the foreign key, it is what turns the key into the documented answer. Removing it, the insert raises Postgres 23503: I called `insertMessage(db, randomUUID(), …)` directly and got `insert or update on table "messages" violates foreign key constraint "messages_room_id_fkey"`. That is not an HTTPException, so app.ts:16-19 `respondToFailure` maps it to `failWith(c, "internal_error", 500)` — breaking routes.test.ts:158-168 (`answers 404 when writing a room that does not exist`) and PRD FR-8, which requires "a 4xx with a safe body, never a crash" for an unknown room. The suggested `INSERT … SELECT FROM rooms WHERE id = $1` returns zero rows for both "room missing" and "id already taken", so the failure path still needs the extra queries; the only saving is on the happy path, where the guard measures p95 0.095 ms cold and 0.227 ms against a 50,000-row table, inside a POST whose whole p95 is 0.34 ms. "Rooms are never deleted" is also asserted rather than enforced — migration 0001 declares `room_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES rooms(id) ON DELETE CASCADE`, i.e. deletion is anticipated by the schema.

verdicts.evidence: Both behaviours are deliberate, documented and already tested. architecture.md §3: "A conflict returns no row, so the stored message is read back scoped to the room: the first write wins and is answered again, while an id already spent in another room is a collision, answered 409 rather than by handing over that room's message", and the §4 table repeats it per endpoint. queries.ts:29-34 says the same thing above the type. The same-room case is a named passing test — queries.test.ts:72-85, "keeps the first text when the same id comes back with a different body", asserting `{ outcome: "already-stored", message: { username: "radu", body: "first" } }` — and the cross-room case is queries.test.ts:87 plus routes.test.ts:94. I ran both over the HTTP surface: replaying an id in its own room with `{username: "mallory", body: "different"}` answers 200 with the stored `{username: "radu", body: "hello"}` and publishes nothing; the same id aimed at another room answers `409 message_id_taken`. That is one rule, not two verdicts — an idempotency key is honoured where it was spent and refused where it was not — and the two answers differ precisely so that room B's caller is not handed room A's content. There is no leak either way: the body handed back is a message of the room the caller is already reading, and history is public (no auth, PRD §4). Nor can the client produce the case: apps/web/src/messages/message-actions.ts:12-13 `composeMessage` mints `randomUuid()` per submission, and the composer retries by calling `onSend` again (message-composer.tsx:40), which composes a fresh id.
verdicts.repro: npx vitest run apps/server/test/messages/queries.test.ts -t "same id"  # the two cases the finding calls contradictory are both green and both named in the spec
verdicts.fix: None. Comparing the whole row and answering 409 on a mismatch would break the retry contract in PRD FR-8 ("a retried message with the same id is stored once") for the exact case it exists for: a retry whose body the client trimmed differently.
verdicts.note: First-write-wins inside the room and 409 across rooms is the documented rule in architecture.md §3, tested at queries.test.ts:72 and :87; the client cannot reuse an id anyway, since every submission mints a new one.
verdicts.originalIssue: The idempotency read-back is scoped by room, so an id reused in another room is a 409 collision while the same id reused in the same room with a different body is a 200 carrying the earlier row: two different verdicts on the same event.

verdicts.evidence: I measured the sweep with the production settings (capacity 40, refill 2/s, forgetAbove 10,000), spraying 200,000 distinct addresses at several arrival rates. At 500/s: 0.00024 ms per request, store settles at 4,980. At 2,000/s: 0.00023 ms, 1,978. At 5,000/s: 0.00019 ms, 4,975. At 20,000/s: 0.187 ms, store pinned at 10,001. The cliff is exactly where the arithmetic puts it: a bucket that spent one token refills in capacity/refill-per-token = 0.5 s, so 10,000 buckets stay non-full only when 10,000/0.5 s = 20,000 distinct addresses arrive every second. Below that the sweep frees (10,000 − rate/2) entries and does not run again until they refill, so it is amortised O(1) — at 5,000/s it costs less per request than at 500/s. 20,000 distinct-source requests a second is 400x NFR-3's tested ceiling of 50 messages/s and a rate at which the process is saturated by ordinary routing regardless; and in the production shape docs/infra-and-cost.md §4 prescribes, every request arrives from the platform proxy, so the store holds one entry and the branch never runs (candidate 21). The suggested fix is worse than the finding: caller-allowances.ts:28-29 returns a known bucket without re-inserting it, so Map order is first-seen order, not least-recently-used — 'evict the oldest at the cap' would evict a caller currently being throttled and hand it a fresh 40 tokens, turning a CPU concern into a rate-limit bypass an attacker triggers on demand by spraying 10,000 addresses.

verdicts.evidence: The compiled stylesheet settles the box model with no browser needed. From the production CSS: `*,:after,:before,::backdrop{box-sizing:border-box}` (preflight), `.h-peek{height:var(--spacing-peek)}` with `--spacing-peek:4.5rem`, `.pb-\[env\(safe-area-inset-bottom\)\]{padding-bottom:env(safe-area-inset-bottom)}`, `.shrink-0{flex-shrink:0}`, `.overflow-hidden{overflow:hidden}`. room-panel.tsx:127-130 puts all of `overflow-hidden`, `border-t`, `pb-[env(safe-area-inset-bottom)]` and the collapsed `h-peek` on one `<section>`, and its only sized in-flow child (line 132) is `flex h-peek shrink-0`. So with a 34px inset the section is a 72px border box: 1px border + 71px padding box − 34px padding = a 37px content box holding a 72px `flex-shrink:0` child. The padding reserves nothing; it only pushes the child's overflow down. The child is `items-center`, its column is `text-lg` (28px) over `text-xs` (16px) = 44px, centred in 72px, so the preview line's bottom edge lands 13px above the physical viewport bottom — entirely inside the 34px strip the padding exists to keep clear. `index.html` carries `viewport-fit=cover`, so the inset is live. The expanded branch is fine: `h-sheet` (70dvh) with a `min-h-0 flex-1` body, so the padding does reserve space there. Above 768px `md:h-auto md:pb-0` removes both. Three details of the candidate are wrong: the 1px `overflow-hidden` clip falls on empty space below the centred column, so nothing visible is cut; index.css:51's `bottom: var(--spacing-peek)` is *correct today* (the collapsed sheet really is 72px tall including the inset) and only needs changing once the sheet grows; and the "iOS eats the first touch" part is about the bottom edge band, which I cannot verify here — the solid, spec-determined part is the content sitting inside the reserved strip.
verdicts.fix: Let the inset sit outside the peek's own height. In room-panel.tsx:130 make the collapsed branch `h-[calc(var(--spacing-peek)+env(safe-area-inset-bottom))]` (keep `h-sheet` for expanded, whose body flexes), leaving the inner row at `h-peek`. Then lift the tile credit by the same amount so it still clears the sheet: index.css:51 becomes `bottom: calc(var(--spacing-peek) + env(safe-area-inset-bottom))`. jsdom cannot see this, so the regression evidence is the page above, not a vitest case.
verdicts.note: Real, and only on a device with a bottom inset: with the section's height pinned to `h-peek`, `pb-[env(safe-area-inset-bottom)]` shrinks the content box instead of reserving a strip, so the collapsed peek's newest-message line — the thing §12 says the peek exists to carry — ends up 13px from the physical bottom edge, inside the 34px area FR-10 asks to be honoured.
verdicts.originalIssue: `h-peek` is the sheet's total border-box height and `pb-[env(safe-area-inset-bottom)]` is inside it, so on a device with a bottom inset the collapsed sheet's usable content box shrinks to 4.5rem − inset while its only child is a fixed `h-peek` (4.5rem) — the peek's content is pushed into the reserved strip instead of clear of it, which is the opposite of what the padding is for.
